59.full_text_basis: Full NeurIPS paper and appendices reviewed; Visualization-of-Thought prompting, natural-language/visual navigation and visual-tiling task construction, dataset sizes, Table 1 comparisons, visualization-quality analysis, weaker-model experiments, difficulty analysis and qualitative failure cases checked.
59.evidence: Visualization-of-Thought (VoT) prompts an LLM to externalize a visual state after each reasoning step so subsequent spatial reasoning can condition on that evolving representation. The experiments cover natural-language navigation plus visual navigation and visual tiling in 2D grid worlds; the visual-navigation data include 496 route-planning maps and 2,520 next-step instances, while visual tiling contains 376 configurations and 796 QA instances. GPT-4 with VoT improves route-planning completion from 37.02% (CoT) to 40.77% and success from 9.48% to 14.72%, next-step prediction from 48.61% to 55.28%, visual tiling from 54.15% to 63.94%, and natural-language navigation from 54.00% to 59.00%. The paper also shows that generated visualizations are imperfect: compliance is about 51–52% and visualization accuracy about 24–26%, although correct visualizations often support correct downstream decisions.
59.limitations: The main tasks are synthetic 2D navigation/tiling settings rather than general real-world environments. VoT depends on the model's ability to generate a usable spatial representation; language/visualization inconsistencies and spatial hallucinations remain common, and the paper reports a ring-navigation case where ordinary CoT outperforms VoT (52.5% versus 49.5%).

797.source: ACM Computing Surveys 58(10), 2026 / DOI 10.1145/3794858 full 44-page article
797.full_text_basis: Full 44-page CSUR article reviewed; formal definition and boundaries of agent generalizability, stakeholder view, benchmark/dataset/task/metric survey, backbone/component/interaction improvement taxonomy, generalizable-framework versus generalizable-agent distinction, open problems and conclusion checked.
797.evidence: The survey defines LLM-agent generalizability as maintaining consistently high performance across varied user instructions, environments, tasks and domains, especially conditions different from fine-tuning data. It separates measurement into datasets, task setups and metrics, then organizes improvement methods into three levels: the backbone LLM, specialized agent components such as perception/memory/tools, and interactions between the backbone and those components. A key conceptual distinction is between a generalizable framework—an architecture or method reusable across settings—and a generalizable agent that actually maintains performance across those settings. The article argues for standardized hierarchical task/domain coverage, variance- and cost-aware metrics, and combined architecture/method interventions instead of inferring generalizability from one benchmark score.
797.limitations: This is a synthesis article rather than a new controlled benchmark, and it explicitly identifies the absence of a universally accepted domain/task ontology and standardized generalizability metrics as an unresolved field-level problem. Its taxonomy necessarily reflects literature available up to the review period and cannot by itself prove cross-domain generalization for any individual agent.

799.source: NAACL 2025 System Demonstrations / ACL Anthology 2025.naacl-demo.17 full paper
799.full_text_basis: Full CowPilot archival paper reviewed; collaborative-control design, suggest/execute and pause/reject/resume mechanisms, 27-task WebArena evaluation, GPT-4o and Llama-3-8B comparisons, human intervention measurements, task-success results, analysis and limitations checked.
799.evidence: CowPilot studies mixed-initiative web navigation where the agent and a human can alternate control instead of forcing a binary choice between full automation and manual browsing. On a 27-task WebArena subset, GPT-4o autonomous execution succeeds on 0.48 of tasks, while CowPilot with human intervention reaches 0.95; the human-only condition reaches 0.89. Humans perform only 1.14 actions on average—15.2% of the collaborative trajectory—while the agent performs 84.8%. The benefit is even larger for a weaker Llama-3-8B agent (0.04 autonomous versus 0.81 collaborative), though it requires substantially more human intervention. The results show that sparse human corrections can recover many grounding/planning failures without discarding agent autonomy.
799.limitations: The study uses only 27 WebArena tasks and three author-evaluators, with humans continuously observing execution. The authors note possible task-ordering effects and that intervention behavior varies by user; broader participant demographics, websites and less attentive supervision are needed before generalizing the collaboration gains.

801.full_text_basis: Full Agent A/B paper reviewed; six-practitioner formative study, end-to-end persona/experiment/interaction pipeline, live-Amazon case study, 100,000 persona pool, 1,000-agent between-subject simulation, parallel 2M-user human experiment, behavior/cost analysis, discussion and conclusion checked.
801.evidence: Agent A/B uses persona-conditioned LLM agents to pilot interface experiments on live websites before or alongside costly human traffic. The system design is grounded in interviews with six industry A/B-testing practitioners. In its Amazon filter-panel case study, the authors generate 100,000 personas and sample 1,000 Claude-3.5-Sonnet agents, 500 per condition, then compare their behavior with a parallel live experiment involving roughly 2 million human users. Agents are more goal-directed and less exploratory than humans but reproduce the direction of the interface effect: the reduced-filter treatment yields 414 agent purchases versus 404 in control (chi-square 5.51, p=0.03). The 1,000-agent run is estimated at 875M tokens, about $2,925 and 35 kg CO2, illustrating both scalability and non-trivial simulation cost.
801.limitations: The paper positions agent simulation as a complement to, not a replacement for, human A/B testing. Its strongest validation is one Amazon shopping redesign using one principal LLM backend; agents show less exploratory behavior than humans, so fidelity across other domains, models, cultural groups and interface changes remains an open question.

811.full_text_basis: Full paper reviewed; 14-task/six-site controlled web testbed, 12 value/preference personas, four agent systems, value/preference alignment coding, promotional-UI intervention, statistical analysis, reasoning-pattern analysis, discussion and explicit limitations checked.
811.evidence: The Behavioral Fabric study tests how explicit user values/preferences and interface cues shape web-agent trajectories. The controlled testbed contains 14 interactive tasks across six replica shopping, travel, dining and housing sites, 12 value/preference personas, and four state-of-the-art agents. Persona guidance changes filter use and decision trajectories, while no-guidance agents show a strong shortest-path efficiency bias. Promotional UI cues such as discounts/bestseller badges can override value-consistent exploration: for GPT-4o, mean steps in value-conditioned tasks fall from 5.86 without promotion to 2.60 with promotion (t=6.13, p<.001, Hedges' g=-2.21), with similarly large effects for DeepSeek and Claude. Longer trajectories are significantly associated with better alignment (ANOVA F(2,424)=6.53, p=.002), while agents often rationalize promotion-driven choices as if they reflected the requested value.
811.limitations: The authors primarily use Browser-use as the interaction framework, employ fixed promotional cues, and study a bounded set of replica sites/tasks. Results depend on prompt/persona construction; externalized reasoning is not direct evidence of latent cognition, and the chosen human-value framework is incomplete and culturally limited.
